summaries.example: Imagine that a trusted messenger says, “Mia will choose the blue book tomorrow.” If Mia is truly free to choose either book, we can ask: does the messenger’s perfect statement make her choice no longer free? Philosophers use puzzles like this to think about prophecy, time, and choice.
summaries.summary: Prophecy is usually understood as a special way that information or guidance from God reaches people. Philosophers focus especially on prophecies about future events that could happen or fail to happen. Their puzzle is this: if God cannot be wrong, and a prophecy becomes part of the past, does the predicted event have to happen? If it has to happen, can a person still choose freely? The entry describes several possible answers. One answer says that all events are already determined, so there are no truly open future choices. Another, called open theism, says God does not know every contingent future event. Ockhamism says the prophecy’s past existence is fixed, while what it reveals might have been different if the person had chosen differently. A different view says God knows events from outside ordinary time. Middle knowledge says God knows what free people would do in any possible situation and can use that knowledge in planning a world. Each answer has supporters and difficult questions.
key_ideas: Prophecy is not always a prediction. It can also make God’s wishes or instructions clearer.
A central puzzle asks how a future free choice can stay open if an unfailing prophecy already says what will happen.
Some thinkers deny that the future contains genuinely open choices.
Others say God does not know every free future choice, or explain divine knowledge using time, the past, or middle knowledge.
The entry studies these ideas without deciding whether any particular historical prophecy really came true.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic connects ideas that affect how people think about God, time, truth, and responsibility. It shows that one simple-sounding sentence about the future can raise hard questions about whether the future is open and whether human choices are genuinely free. The discussion also models how philosophers compare different explanations without settling questions about religion or particular prophecies.

important_terms.definition: A message connected with the divine, often understood as sharing God’s will or information with people.
Something that might happen but also might not happen. A free choice is often treated as an example.
The ability to choose and act for yourself rather than being forced by something outside you.
Knowing something before it happens.
The view that God knows what people would freely do in many different situations.

questions_to_think_about: If someone knows your choice perfectly, does that knowledge force you to choose it?
Can a message about the future be a warning or instruction instead of a prediction?
Would a choice still be free if you could not choose another way?
What might God need to know in order to guide events?

summaries.example: Suppose an infallible prophecy says that Elena will freely sign a petition tomorrow. At the time of the prophecy, her signing seems contingent: she could sign or refuse. Yet the prophecy is now a past fact, and a past fact seems unchangeable. Does the truth of the prophecy make refusal impossible, or would the prophecy itself have been different if Elena had freely refused? This is the structure of the philosophical problem.
summaries.summary: The entry examines prophecy mainly as a philosophical test case for divine knowledge and human freedom, not as an investigation into whether particular prophecies were fulfilled. A prophecy about a future contingent event creates a three-part problem: God is infallible, the predicted event appears genuinely open, and the prophecy becomes part of the unalterable past. One response denies contingency through determinism or a compatibilist account of freedom. Open theism instead denies that God knows all contingent future truths, while attempting to explain prophecy through conditional warnings, evidence from present tendencies, or divine decisions about God’s own future actions. Ockhamism separates the necessity of the past utterance from the contingency of its content, sometimes implying counterfactual power over the past. The atemporal-eternity approach says God knows all times without being earlier than the events known, but it faces the question of how a temporal prophecy affects later freedom. Molinism distinguishes natural, middle, and free knowledge: God knows necessary truths, what free creatures would do in possible circumstances, and truths dependent on divine choice. This may support providential control while retaining contingency, but philosophers dispute whether freedom-counterfactuals have determinate truth values or adequate grounds.
key_ideas: The philosophical problem adds a past prophecy to the familiar problem of reconciling divine knowledge with future contingency and freedom.
Denying future contingency solves part of the puzzle, but it may conflict with views that treat free choice as requiring genuine alternatives.
Open theism preserves future contingency by restricting divine knowledge, but its account of prophetic prediction raises questions about probability, trends, and specifically predicted actions.

Ockhamist proposals distinguish the necessity of the past event of prophesying from the alleged necessity of what the prophecy concerns; critics question whether this gives agents unusual power over the past.
The atemporal view replaces foreknowledge in the temporal sense with timeless knowledge, yet critics argue that a prophecy made in time still seems to threaten contingency.

Molinism combines natural knowledge of necessities, middle knowledge of counterfactuals of freedom, and free knowledge of truths dependent on God’s decision; critics ask what makes such counterfactuals true and knowable.
summaries.why_it_matters: The problem of prophecy brings together metaphysics, philosophy of religion, theories of time, theories of truth, and debates about free will. It clarifies why simply saying that God knows the future is not enough: philosophers must explain whether that knowledge is temporal or timeless, whether the future is already settled, and how prophecy relates to a fixed past. Comparing the proposed solutions also reveals trade-offs between divine control, divine knowledge, and robust human freedom. The entry presents these disagreements without deciding the underlying theological questions.

important_terms.definition: A person understood as mediating divine communication or guidance to other people; prophecy need not involve forecasting.
An event that is neither guaranteed to occur nor guaranteed not to occur, including a possible future free action.
The thesis that every event is fixed by prior sufficient conditions, leaving no genuinely open alternatives in the relevant sense.
Knowledge of an event possessed before that event occurs in time; the article distinguishes this from timeless knowledge.
The position that God does not know some future contingent truths, because they are not yet settled, unknowable, or deliberately left unknown.
A family of views associated with Ockham holding that a past prophecy is fixed while its content need not be necessary; this can involve dependence of the past on a future free act.
The view that God is not located at an earlier moment observing later events, but knows all events from a timeless perspective.
On Molina’s account, knowledge of contingent truths about what free agents would do in specified possible circumstances.

questions_to_think_about: Does an infallible statement about a future choice make the choice necessary, or does it merely describe what the agent will do?
Can a past fact be fixed while its content depends counterfactually on a later free action?
Would timeless knowledge avoid the problem, or does the temporal act of prophecy recreate it?
What would ground the truth of a counterfactual saying what someone would freely do in a situation they never actually face?
Is freedom compatible with an inevitable action if the action arises from the agent’s own desires rather than external compulsion?

summaries.example: Imagine a coach who never makes a mistake saying, “You will choose to join the chess team tomorrow.” You still feel that you can choose chess or another club. But after the coach has said it, the statement is part of the past. Did the coach’s perfect knowledge force your choice? Or would the coach have said something different if you had freely chosen another club? Philosophers use this kind of puzzle to study prophecy.
summaries.summary: Prophecy can mean making divine purposes clear, but philosophers often study a narrower case: a prophecy that accurately describes a future event that seems free and unsettled. This produces a puzzle. If God cannot be mistaken, and the prophecy is now a past fact, does the future event have to occur? If it must occur, how could it still be a free choice? The entry presents several approaches. Some deny that future contingent events exist, perhaps because everything is determined or because freedom does not require real alternatives. Open theism keeps an open future by limiting what God knows about it; proposed explanations of prophecy include conditional messages, predictions based on current tendencies, and revelations of God’s own future actions. Ockhamism says the past act of prophesying is fixed, while the event described need not be necessary. The timeless view says God knows all events without being earlier than them. Middle knowledge says God knows what free people would do in possible circumstances and chooses a world accordingly. Each proposal faces objections, so the article compares them rather than choosing a final answer.
key_ideas: Prophets may communicate God’s purposes, not just tell people what will happen later.
The main puzzle concerns whether an unerring prophecy makes a supposedly free future event unavoidable.
One response says every event is determined, so future choices are not open in the strongest sense.
Open theism protects an open future by saying God does not know all future choices; other thinkers explain the issue through the past, timelessness, or middle knowledge.
Philosophers disagree about whether these solutions preserve both God’s knowledge and meaningful human freedom.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate matters because it asks how several important ideas fit together: divine communication, knowledge, time, choice, and responsibility. It also teaches a useful philosophical habit: instead of arguing about whether a particular prophecy was genuine, thinkers can examine an ideal case and test the logic carefully. The different answers show that protecting one idea—such as an open future—may require changing how we understand another, such as divine knowledge or the power of the past.

important_terms.definition: A special message or role through which people are told about divine purposes, instructions, or sometimes future events.
An event that is not settled one way or the other; it could happen, but it could also fail to happen.
The power to make choices that are genuinely your own, rather than choices completely fixed by outside causes.
Knowledge of something before it happens. Divine foreknowledge means God knows future events in advance.
The view that the future is not fully settled and that God does not know every future contingent event.
A proposal that the past prophecy is fixed, but what it reports might have been different if a person had freely acted differently.
The idea that God is outside ordinary time and knows past, present, and future together rather than waiting for events to occur.
Knowledge of what a free person would do in different possible situations, used in one theory of divine planning.

questions_to_think_about: If a perfect prediction cannot be wrong, does it cause the event or simply report it?
Could a warning about what may happen count as prophecy even if it is conditional?
Does knowing what someone would do in a situation differ from knowing what they will actually do?
Can an action be free if it is certain to happen?
